messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Juan, a 35-year-old Latin American musician, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that left him feeling deeply scarred and disoriented. Married and part of a vibrant community, Juan's world was shattered when he was involved in a serious car crash on his way to a concert. The trauma of the event is evident in how it continues to impact every aspect of his daily life. Since the accident, Juan finds himself constantly surrounded by people, an effort to keep his mind off the haunting memories that seem to lurk just beneath the surface. He avoids being alone, as even a momentary silence can bring back fragments of the terrifying event. "I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts," he explains, highlighting how socializing has become a coping mechanism. However, this constant need for companionship is driven by his belief that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it. Juan feels like his life has been destroyed, and the injustice of the situation fuels his fear of losing control over his emotions. "What happened to me was deeply unfair," he says, convinced that he might not be able to contain his anger if left alone with his thoughts. The trauma itself is a fragmented experience for Juan. He recalls bits and pieces of the accident but struggles to piece them together into a coherent narrative. When he tries to deliberately remember what happened, it feels like the memory is just out of reach. "When I try to deliberately remember what happened, I find it difficult to access the memory," he notes. The fragmented nature of his recollections further exacerbates his sense of injustice and fear. Each fragment that comes back feels like a piece of evidence reinforcing how his life was irrevocably altered. This difficulty in recalling the event clearly has led Juan to avoid talking or thinking about it altogether. He dreads the conversations with friends and family who might bring up the accident, as each mention triggers another jolt of memory. The fragmented memories also contribute to his constant state of avoidance; he is certain that if he delves into these recollections, they will only lead him back to feelings of rage and helplessness. Juan’s music career has been profoundly affected by this cycle. As a musician, he often performs alone on stage, which used to be his sanctuary. Now, the solitude of the performance space triggers flashbacks that disrupt his focus and leave him feeling vulnerable. "Being alone with my instrument makes me feel like I'm reliving it all over again," he says, highlighting how even his professional life has become intertwined with his trauma. The fear that Juan will not be able to control his anger adds another layer of tension in his interactions with others. He worries that a moment of silence might lead him to explode, and so he clings to social situations as a safety net. This constant need for company is both a coping mechanism and a symptom of his underlying beliefs about the unfairness of his situation. What has finally brought Juan to seek help is the realization that these strategies are not sustainable in the long term. His marriage feels strained, and the avoidance behaviors have begun to impact his ability to perform and connect with others authentically. He hopes for a way to regain control over his thoughts and emotions without having to be constantly surrounded by people. Juan’s most pressing fear is that he will never fully understand or integrate what happened to him, leaving him trapped in a cycle of fragmented memories and avoidance behaviors. At the same time, he is hopeful that with help, he can find a way to navigate through his trauma and reclaim some semblance of peace and control over his life.
